title: Government faces $15b cyber security overhaul to stop AI
key_facts: Hamish Hansford, a senior Home Affairs official, told a protective security and government conference in Canberra that replacing the government's legacy tech estate is a '15, 16, $17 billion proposition' and a 'defining challenge' of the next five years.
He said AI can 'super charge' cyber incidents by finding vulnerabilities in record time that then target operational technology.
Craig Bickell, Home Affairs assistant secretary for Commonwealth security policy, said departments must meet the cost within their allocated budgets.

A directive under the Protective Security Policy Framework, issued the week before, gives departments until December to tell Home Affairs how they will protect critical systems and which will be scrapped and when.
Officials urged live drills ('wargame and test') over rules-based compliance; Home Affairs will issue fewer cyber directives in future.
Stephanie Crowe of the Australian Cyber Security Centre said updates to the Essential Eight standards will be released later this month.
The Australian AI Safety Institute and CSIRO released research on AI oversight, including a tool to measure whether a model's output is correct and whether it influences its users.
quote_evidence: Replacing legacy tech and building cyber security preparedness would be a "defining challenge" of the next five years, Mr Hansford said, with a wholesale overhaul of the government's legacy tech estate representing a "15, 16, $17 billion proposition".
The directive gives departments until December to tell Home Affairs how they will protect critical systems, which will be scrapped and to what timeline.
why_it_matters_hint: An Australian official puts a rough price of $15 to $17 billion on replacing old government IT, to be met from existing budgets, because AI makes weaknesses easier to find.
event_date: Conference on Wednesday 7 Oct 2026 (weekday given in the article, date inferred from its 11 Oct publication)
